primary.date_status: Supplied date; no source ties this date to a specific Manafort action.
primary.description_short: TrumpFile alleges Manafort helped Russia take Crimea in 2014; the supplied Vox link does not name Manafort or establish that role.
primary.description_medium: TrumpFile's March 16, 2014 entry alleges that Paul Manafort helped Russia take control of Crimea through an illegal vote and cites a Vox explainer. The Vox article describes the referendum under Russian military occupation but does not mention Manafort. No supplied source identifies an action by him or connects him to the takeover; keep the allegation unverified.
primary.description_long:
The supplied TrumpFile page labels the event March 16, 2014 and says Russia took control of Crimea “with help from Paul Manafort” through an “illegal vote.” Its only linked reference in the packet is a Vox explainer about the 2014 Ukraine crisis. That article describes Crimea’s March referendum as taking place without international monitors and under Russian military occupation, but it does not name Manafort or attribute a role in the seizure to him.

The available record documents an allegation made by the TrumpFile page, not independent support for Manafort’s alleged assistance. The packet identifies no action, date, intermediary, or mechanism by which he could have aided Russia’s takeover. Manafort’s political work in Ukraine, even where reported, would not by itself establish involvement in Crimea’s occupation or referendum. This draft keeps the supplied allegation visible for review and makes no finding that it occurred.

The March 16 date remains supplied rather than verified as the date of a specific Manafort action. The link to Donald Trump is also unresolved in this event record. To treat the claim as a historical event, a reliable source must identify a specific Manafort action and connect it to Russia’s control of Crimea; otherwise the entry should be narrowed or excluded.

frozen_original.title: Supreme Court Grants Trump Broad Presidential Immunity — Delays All Federal Cases
frozen_original.synopsis: On July 1, 2024, the Supreme Court issued a landmark 6-3 ruling in Trump v. United States, granting former presidents broad immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts conducted while in office. The ruling — the first time the Supreme Court addressed presidential criminal immunity — dramatically narrowed the scope of Special Counsel Jack Smith's federal indictment against Trump related to the 2020 election interference scheme. The decision required lower courts to determine which of Trump's alleged acts were "official" and thus immune, effectively delaying the federal trial past the November 2024 election. Critics argued the ruling placed presidents above the law and created conditions for future authoritarian abuse of power.

frozen_original.title: Trump Threatens to Revoke Tax-Exempt Status of Universities That Don't Comply
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social threatening to revoke the tax-exempt status of universities that refused to comply with his administration's demands on DEI, protest policies, and faculty governance — a threat that, if carried out, would expose elite university endowments worth tens of billions of dollars to taxation and potentially devastate research and scholarship programs. Legal scholars noted such revocations require IRS action and would face enormous legal hurdles, and that threatening tax status to coerce ideological compliance raised serious First Amendment violations. Nevertheless, the threat sent shockwaves through higher education, with university boards convening emergency legal reviews. The IRS's independence from presidential political pressure was already under assault as the administration sought to use tax enforcement as a tool of political intimidation.

Neither establishes the supplied February tax-status claim, so this remains an internal, unverified draft.
primary.description_long: Internal draft only. The supplied card alleges that Donald Trump posted on February 15, 2025, threatening to revoke the tax-exempt status of universities that rejected administration demands concerning DEI, campus protest policies, and faculty governance. The packet contains no original post URL or source excerpt establishing that date, broad university scope, or the stated conditions. Search excerpts surfaced separate February reporting about an Education Department warning that institutions could lose federal funding over DEI, and April reporting about a Harvard-specific tax-status threat. Those reports concern different actions, dates, and scopes; they do not verify this allegation and are not substituted as the event. The supplied text also asserts that endowments worth tens of billions of dollars could be exposed, that research programs faced severe consequences, that legal scholars identified First Amendment problems, that university boards held emergency reviews, and that the threat sent shockwaves through higher education. The packet supplies no supporting excerpts for those details. Preserve the alleged February claim only as attributed, with its date and scope marked uncertain. Publication requires a matching original post or reliable contemporaneous report and source review.

corrected_proposal.description_long: The supplied record alleges that Trump wrote on Truth Social on February 15, 2025 that universities could lose tax-exempt status if they rejected administration demands about DEI, campus protests, and faculty governance. The supplied materials include no matching post or contemporaneous report for that allegation. Separate February reporting concerns an Education Department warning about possible federal-funding consequences for DEI; an April report concerns a tax-status threat to Harvard specifically. Neither verifies the alleged February threat to universities generally. The frozen entry also claims the threat put university endowments and research programs at risk and prompted legal objections and emergency board reviews, but no supporting excerpts for those claims are included. The date, scope, exact wording, and conditions remain unverified. The supplied materials do not show that any university lost tax-exempt status as a result of the alleged threat. Additional proof is needed.

frozen_original.title: Trump executive order expanding indefinite detention without judicial review
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump signed a sweeping executive order expanding the government's authority to hold individuals in indefinite detention without judicial review, fundamentally undermining habeas corpus and due process. The order applied not only to immigrants but was written broadly enough to potentially cover citizens designated as enemy combatants or national security threats at executive discretion. Legal scholars characterized the order as the most direct assault on habeas corpus in American history since its suspension during the Civil War.

primary.decision: Exclude the alleged April 2025 indefinite-detention executive order unless its title, number, or text is supplied. The official April presidential-document index yielded no matching title; the March 15 Alien Enemies Act proclamation is a separate earlier action and is not substituted for the alleged order.

blockers.detail: The frozen record gives no order number, title, text, or citation. The asserted authority to detain indefinitely without judicial review and to reach citizens designated as threats is unsupported.

The Federal Register API returned 58 presidential documents published in April 2025; inspection of the titles found no item matching the alleged detention/habeas order. This title-index search is not proof that unpublished guidance did not exist.

The accessible Alien Enemies Act proclamation is dated March 15, 2025 and describes immediate apprehension, detention, and removal of the defined Alien Enemies. Its date, legal instrument, and described group differ from the alleged April order; it cannot repair this record.
